children: Geet Nazir emphasized the necessity for brands to adapt across different audiences, channels, and markets while remaining anchored to a clear purpose

Brands today operate in an environment where consumer expectations are increasingly fragmented, and businesses are expanding across various markets, categories, and channels. In this landscape, building a resilient brand necessitates more than just a recognisable logo or consistent advertising.

Speaking at The Future of Design Summit & Awards 2026, Geet Nazir, Managing Director of Landor, highlighted that businesses must construct brands capable of adapting to changing contexts while staying connected to their core purpose.

“Markets are expanding, and segments are diversifying. People’s expectations from brands today are fragmented,” Nazir stated. She added that brands now operate across multiple channels, with consumers actively involved in the conversation rather than merely receiving brand communication.
Purpose as a Foundation

According to Nazir, clarity of purpose is a key foundation for brand resilience. A well-defined purpose provides a common direction for both employees and consumers, guiding decisions related to business growth and transformation.

She cited the Taj brand as an example of how purpose can be experienced beyond traditional brand communication. The hospitality brand’s philosophy is reflected in its service, employee behavior, and customer experience.

Nazir also referenced Tata Consumer Products, where the “For Better” platform unifies the organisation’s commitment to quality, consumers, and progress. She explained that purpose can influence aspects such as innovation, packaging, sustainability, and corporate behavior.
“A clear purpose protects brands from drift,” Nazir noted, adding that it can provide a roadmap for growth and help organizations stay aligned with their long-term direction.
When Business Transformation Necessitates a New Identity

Nazir observed that a brand’s identity should evolve when its underlying business changes. This is especially true for legacy companies, where established perceptions may hinder consumers from recognizing the scale or direction of a transformation.

She cited DTDC, which transitioned from being primarily known as a courier company to positioning itself as an integrated express logistics provider. Its new identity aimed to communicate its scale, technology, innovation, and global partnerships while retaining a connection to its heritage.
This example illustrates that a rebrand should not merely be a visual exercise; it should effectively communicate a meaningful change in the business.
Building Recognition Beyond the Logo
For Nazir, resilient branding encompasses creating a broader system of distinctive assets that consumers can recognise without necessarily seeing the company name or logo.

She cited McDonald’s golden arches as a visual asset that has become strongly associated with the brand. In an environment where consumer attention is increasingly fragmented, such assets can help brands achieve faster recognition and stronger memory structures.
Additionally, she referred to the Milan Symphony Orchestra, which used elements associated with the city.
For Tata, Nazir pointed to the “Move With Meaning” platform and its sonic identity as examples of how a brand can build recognition through elements beyond its traditional logo.
Building Brands That Can Adapt

Nazir insisted that brand resilience should not be mistaken for keeping a brand unchanged. Instead, brands must maintain coherence while adapting to different audiences, cultures, channels, and markets.
She outlined five principles for resilient brands:
Business ambition as the value of the brand
Purpose as its compass
Identity as its signal
Distinctive assets as its memory
Adaptability as the means to connect with cultures and communities
For brands operating in India’s diverse market, the challenge is to build systems that can extend across different contexts without losing the central idea that binds the brand together.
Samiksha Choudhary
BW Reporters
The author is a Trainee Correspondent at BW Businessworld.
